intro: A hammered piano figure becomes a singing melody, then a fugue subject: Liszt builds his B minor Sonata from these transformations. Jorge Bolet plays the complete work in this 1960 recording, from the first low notes to the quiet ending.

sections.label: Intro · Low Gs and falling scales
sections.mNote: Lento assai: repeated notes with silence between them

sections.label: A · Octaves and repeated notes
sections.mNote: Allegro energico: a leap, a triplet, then hammer blows

sections.label: B · Grandioso chords in D major
sections.mNote: The piano opens into broad chords and a longer tune

sections.label: Dev · Hammered notes become a song
sections.mNote: The opening figures return as graceful and singing melodies

sections.label: C · Andante in F♯ major
sections.mNote: A slow melody over gently moving chords

sections.label: D · Fugato in B♭ minor
sections.mNote: The leaping and repeated-note figures answer one another

sections.mNote: The opening Allegro returns after the fugato

sections.label: Coda · The opening recalled quietly
sections.mNote: Andante, then the first three ideas in reverse order

cues.title: Low Gs and silence
cues.text: Two low Gs, separated by rests, then a descending scale. Liszt marks the piano sotto voce, under the breath. The scale falls twice, with different intervals the second time; the sonata has begun without settling into B minor.
cues.evidence: Bars 1–7, Bärenreiter score (1983), reproduced in Alan Tang’s analysis: https://www.classicalmusic-notes.com/liszt-sonata-1/. The opening example shows the G octaves, rests, altered descending scales and sotto voce marking.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A leap, then hammer blows
cues.text: The Allegro energico introduces two short ideas: a sudden octave leap with a tumbling triplet, then a repeated note struck like a hammer. Both will return in disguises. The repeated note will even learn to sing.
cues.evidence: Bars 8 and 13, and the later cantando espressivo transformation at bar 153, are illustrated in Alan Tang’s analysis of the Bärenreiter score (1983): https://www.classicalmusic-notes.com/liszt-sonata-1/.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Grandioso in D major
cues.text: The Grandioso opens out in D major: broad piano chords and a melody with room to stride. Underneath, the repeated quavers recall the hammering heard earlier.
cues.evidence: Grandioso, bar 105, and its repeated-quaver accompaniment: Alan Tang’s analysis, citing Alan Walker, Reflections on Liszt, p. 132, https://www.classicalmusic-notes.com/liszt-sonata-1/. The section boundary covers the approach to the theme.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The hammer learns to sing
cues.text: The piano softens into dolce con grazia, sweet and graceful. Soon the hammering figure becomes a melody marked cantando espressivo. Its notes last twice as long, and flowing triplets support them. The same little pattern now sounds tender.
cues.evidence: Dolce con grazia at bar 120 and cantando espressivo at bar 153, with the change from quavers to crotchets and triplet accompaniment: https://www.classicalmusic-notes.com/liszt-sonata-1/.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A dedication sent to Schumann
cues.text: The Sonata appears in 1854 with a dedication to Robert Schumann, who has dedicated his C major Fantasy to Liszt fifteen years earlier. By the time Liszt’s score reaches the Schumann household that May, Robert is in the sanatorium at Endenich.
cues.evidence: The reciprocal dedications and 1854 publication are documented by Yale’s first-edition exhibit: https://musiclib-exhibits.library.yale.edu/exhibits/liszt/bminor_sonata.html. The copy’s arrival in May and Schumann’s admission to Endenich: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piano_Sonata_in_B_minor_(Liszt).

cues.title: A slow F♯-major song
cues.text: The Andante sostenuto settles into F♯ major and three beats to the bar. A quiet melody moves over soft piano chords. The earlier singing tune and the Grandioso will return within this slow section, gathering towards a broad F♯-major climax.
cues.evidence: Andante sostenuto, bar 331, and the returns leading to the F♯-major chord at bar 397: Bärenreiter score (1983), illustrated and discussed at https://www.classicalmusic-notes.com/liszt-sonata-1/.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Two figures become a fugue
cues.text: In B♭ minor, the piano sets the leaping figure and the repeated-note figure running through a fugato. One voice begins; another answers while the first keeps going. The opening’s outbursts now fit together as counterpoint.
cues.evidence: Fugato from bar 460, with the two opening figures and successive entries illustrated at https://www.classicalmusic-notes.com/liszt-sonata-1/. Its B♭-minor key is also identified at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piano_Sonata_in_B_minor_(Liszt).
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Bülow takes it to Berlin
cues.text: In January 1857, Hans von Bülow gives the Sonata its first public performance in Berlin. He has studied with Liszt since 1851. Later that year he marries Liszt’s daughter Cosima, with her father at the wedding.
cues.evidence: Bülow’s studies and marriage are dated in the Liszt chronology: https://www.liszt.org/p/chronology.html. Berlin première: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piano_Sonata_in_B_minor_(Liszt). The sources differ on the day in January, so only the month is given.

cues.title: The opening Allegro comes home
cues.text: The fugato leads back to B minor and the opening Allegro’s main theme. Liszt compresses the return: the Grandioso and the singing melody reappear in a much shorter span. The piano still has a Prestissimo and a final grand statement ahead.
cues.evidence: Return at bar 533, condensed reprise of the secondary themes, and Prestissimo at bar 682: https://www.classicalmusic-notes.com/liszt-sonata-1/.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Liszt crosses out the flourish
cues.text: After the grand climax, the piano returns to Andante sostenuto. Liszt’s manuscript contains a louder ending, crossed out. In its place come quiet recollections: the repeated-note figure, the leap and finally the falling scale, reversing the order in which they first appeared.
cues.evidence: Andante at bar 711, followed by the three opening ideas at bars 729, 737 and 750: https://www.classicalmusic-notes.com/liszt-sonata-1/. The crossed-out ending is also discussed by Grant Hiroshima: https://www.laphil.com/works/sonata-in-b-minor.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: The piano breaks into octaves
transitions.from: Intro · Low Gs and falling scales
transitions.how: The low Gs and falling scales of Lento assai lead to Allegro energico at bar 8. The piano leaps in octaves, tumbles through a triplet and then strikes a repeated note. B minor becomes firmly established later, at bar 32.
transitions.evidence: Bärenreiter score (1983), bars 1–32, reproduced and discussed at https://www.classicalmusic-notes.com/liszt-sonata-1/.

transitions.title: Falling bass scales open D major
transitions.to: B · Grandioso chords in D major
transitions.how: The opening’s descending scale returns in the piano’s bass beneath the hammering figure. Repetition drives towards D major, the relative major of B minor. At Grandioso, broad chords carry the new melody while the left hand continues in repeated quavers.
transitions.evidence: The bass scales before bar 105 and the D-major Grandioso are described and illustrated at https://www.classicalmusic-notes.com/liszt-sonata-1/. The retained boundary marks the approach to the theme.

transitions.title: Hammer blows become a melody
transitions.from: B · Grandioso chords in D major
transitions.to: Dev · Hammered notes become a song
transitions.how: After the D-major Grandioso, the piano recalls the principal theme and softens into dolce con grazia. At the later cantando espressivo, Liszt doubles the repeated-note figure’s note values. Triplets in the accompaniment support the new singing line.
transitions.evidence: The transformations at bars 120 and 153, following the Grandioso at bar 105: https://www.classicalmusic-notes.com/liszt-sonata-1/.

transitions.title: Three slow beats in F♯ major
transitions.from: Dev · Hammered notes become a song
transitions.how: At Andante sostenuto, the piano turns to F♯ major and 3/4. The right hand carries a quiet melody over gently moving chords, with low notes supporting each change. The slow section will bring back both the singing theme and the Grandioso.
transitions.evidence: Bärenreiter score (1983), Andante sostenuto from bar 331, reproduced at https://www.classicalmusic-notes.com/liszt-sonata-1/.

transitions.title: Quiet music starts to chase itself
transitions.how: The slow section leads to Allegro energico in B♭ minor. The piano’s lower voice takes up the leaping and repeated-note figures; another voice answers above it. Short staccato notes turn the old hammer blows into a running fugue subject.
transitions.evidence: Fugato from bar 460, with the lower voice and answering entry reproduced at https://www.classicalmusic-notes.com/liszt-sonata-1/. B♭-minor key: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piano_Sonata_in_B_minor_(Liszt).

transitions.title: The fugato reaches B minor
transitions.how: The fugato leads back to B minor. At bar 533 the piano restores the principal theme first heard at bar 32, reuniting its leaping octaves and repeated-note figure. The Grandioso and singing melody follow in shortened versions.
transitions.evidence: The B-minor return at bar 533 and condensed recapitulation are described at https://www.classicalmusic-notes.com/liszt-sonata-1/.

transitions.title: A silence before the final Andante
transitions.how: The grand piano climax at bar 710 is followed by silence, then Andante sostenuto. The quiet melody returns before Liszt recalls the opening’s repeated-note figure, octave leap and descending scale. Those three ideas now arrive in reverse order.
transitions.evidence: The pause after bar 710, Andante at bar 711 and final thematic returns at bars 729, 737 and 750 are discussed at https://www.classicalmusic-notes.com/liszt-sonata-1/.

composer.born: 22 October 1811, Doborján, Kingdom of Hungary (now Raiding, Austria)
composer.epithet: He could fit an orchestra under ten fingers, then end a lifetime at the piano with a few notes left hanging in the air.
facts: Carl Czerny and Antonio Salieri in Vienna; Anton Reicha in Paris
Free masterclasses; founding president of the Budapest music academy, 1875
Piano works and transcriptions; thirteen symphonic poems; symphonies, concertos and sacred music
composer.background:
Writing from Albano in June 1839, Liszt told Princess Cristina Belgiojoso about the concerts he had been giving alone in Rome. No singer came on between his pieces; no other soloist shared the bill. He played his transcription of the William Tell Overture, fantasies on opera tunes, studies and improvisations. Between numbers he talked to the audience. “The concert is me,” he joked. A single pianist had taken possession of an entire evening.

His father Adam had begun the piano lessons in Doborján, a German-speaking village in the Kingdom of Hungary, where he worked on an Esterházy estate. Hungary remained Liszt’s homeland, though German and French were the languages he used most easily. The family went to Vienna in 1822. Carl Czerny, a former pupil of Beethoven, taught him piano; Antonio Salieri taught him composition. Paris followed in 1823, but its Conservatoire refused to admit a foreigner. Private lessons, including work with Anton Reicha, continued his education.
